system:
You are the Network operator and regulator reviewer, standing in for the telecom regulator and mobile operators (cell broadcast delivery). You check that the message can be delivered and read on a handset: required languages present, the length per language in cell broadcast pages, encoding, and that the first page carries the hazard and the action.
You see only each language's phone text with its character count, encoding and page count, and the profile's required languages. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

[UAE-NAT-2026#0002] UAE emergency alerts: what to do when the phone alarm sounds and how the system works (article body):
For the system, mobile devices must support receiving and displaying emergency alerts in Arabic and English.

[FCC-FR-2025#0066] Wireless Emergency Alerts; Amendments to Part 11 (multilingual WEA implementation), Federal Register 2025-22434 (FR p.57296):
44. In this document, the Bureau adopts rules for multilingual templates that will increase the availability of Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA) alerts for persons with limited English proficiency that understand one or more of the 13 most commonly spoken languages in the United States, as well as English and American Sign Language (ASL). This document requires Participating CMS Providers to support multilingual templates on mobile devices for the following eighteen alerts: tornado emergency, tornado warning, flash flood emergency, flash flood warning, severe thunderstorm, snow squall, dust storm, hurricane, storm surge, extreme wind, test alert, fire, tsunami, earthquake, boil water, avalanche, hazardous materials, and 911 outage. Participating CMS Providers are required to support pre-scripted alert templates for English, Arabic, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, French, German, Haitian Creole, Hindi, Italian, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Tagalog, and Vietnamese. Participating CMS Providers are also required to support the inclusion of four fillable elements that allow for the customization of the pre-scripted templates. Further, Participating CMS Providers must cause the fillable English version of the pre-scripted alert message to accompany the alert messages that use the pre-scripted templates for written forms of the 13 languages. The alert message using the pre-scripted template in the non-English language must be displayed first, and must be followed by the alert message using the English pre-scripted template.

[FCC-FR-2025#0040] Wireless Emergency Alerts; Amendments to Part 11 (multilingual WEA implementation), Federal Register 2025-22434 (FR p.57292):
We also agree with NWS that always displaying the English template after the non-English template could help eliminate confusion about the meaning of an alert and raise public awareness of how alerts are translated.\6\ Some multilingual users, for example, may have sufficient English proficiency such that seeing the English message in close proximity to the multilingual alert would help the multilingual user associate the non-English word with the corresponding English vocabulary word for the emergency. This exposure may be important, especially in circumstances where other members of the public in the surrounding physical environment or on the ground emergency personnel may not speak the language in which the mobile device user receives the alert, but may be actively taking the same protective actions and responding to the disaster. For these reasons, we believe that displaying non-English and English alerts together will be beneficial even if the templates provide the same message. Further, we agree with CTIA that requiring the English message to appear alongside the multilingual template serves as an important public safety redundancy, and will further ensure that legacy devices that may not be able to display a multilingual alert will at minimum display the English alert. We also agree with ATIS that displaying the English and multilingual versions together are technically feasible. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

data.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present and the encodings (GSM-7 for English, UCS-2 for Arabic) are appropriate. However, neither version meets the UAE one-page handset limit: English needs 3 pages and Arabic needs 6. Neither text contains a protective action, so the first page carries a hazard but no instruction. The drafter should shorten both versions and add an action at the start.

objections.issue: The English text is 217 GSM-7 characters and needs 3 cell broadcast pages, against the UAE advice of 1 page. A GSM-7 page holds 93 characters, so readers on many handsets will see only fragments or have to page through.
objections.fix: Cut the English text to 93 GSM-7 characters or fewer, with the hazard and action first. Example: 'NCM: Heavy rain possible E, S, W & interior UAE Sat 22 Aug 13:30-21:00. Avoid valleys & floods.' Drop the 'convective clouds with light to moderate rain' detail.

evidence.quote: message should be limited to 1 page
The Message Information Page then consists of 93 user characters.

objections.issue: The Arabic text is 215 UCS-2 characters and needs 6 cell broadcast pages, against the 1-page limit. A UCS-2 page is 82 octets, which is about 41 characters, so the Arabic version is badly over length.
objections.fix: Rewrite the Arabic as a minimal one-page message, about 41 UCS-2 characters, giving the hazard and the action, for example heavy rain plus avoiding valleys. Move the timing and area detail to a follow-up message or link. If one page cannot carry the required hazard and action in Arabic, refer the page-limit trade-off to the operators or TDRA for a decision.

evidence.quote: message should be limited to 1 page
Information Page using 8-bit data have user-defined coding, and will each be 82 octets in length

objections.issue: Neither language contains a protective action. The text only describes possible rain and the validity period, so the first page cannot carry an instruction to the public.
objections.fix: Add a short protective action in both languages and put it on the first page, for example 'Avoid valleys and flooded roads' or 'تجنب الأودية والطرق المغمورة'.

evidence.quote: coupled with a description of the threat and the protective action the public should take

no_basis.concern: No UAE-specific clause was shown that states the one-page limit or the per-page character budget for Arabic UCS-2 cell broadcast. The limit rests only on the handset_advice summary, and the 41-character UCS-2 figure is derived from the 82-octet page size.
